## Summary

Two prompt recipes from an agent-heavy developer, delivered as a deliberate pair (the follow-up opens "people seem to like this so here's another one"):

1. **The 80% simplification pass** (quoted, 2026-09-16): after finishing a planning session with an agent, tell it: *"now come up with a much simpler solution that provides 80% of the benefits we are talking about here."* His claim: "without fail every time it has come up with a much better design."
2. **One-directional dependency refactor** (2026-09-17): agents "love to dump a bunch of files in a single folder with all the implementation all over the place" — so he tells it: *"refactor all this logic into folders with clear dependencies in a single direction."* (Tweet body truncated mid-sentence at capture — syndication API cut; the prompt text itself is complete.)

Both target the same failure mode: agents over-produce — plans accrete features, code accretes files — and a short mechanical prompt forces a compression pass the agent won't do unprompted.

## Why it matters

- **The 80% prompt is forward-implementation-first applied at the planning stage** — [[2026-08-30-forward-implementation-first-skill]] guards execution; Agrawal's prompt guards the plan itself. Same economics: the last 20% of benefit usually costs most of the complexity, and asking for the simpler design *after* the full design exists means the agent knows exactly what it's cutting.
- **Slots at the end of the Phelps loop** ([[2026-09-06-phelps-agentic-planning-loop]]): converge the PRD through multi-model critique, then run the "much simpler, 80% of benefits" pass before anything gets built. Critique finds what's wrong; the simplification prompt asks what's unnecessary.
- **The dependency-direction prompt is a structure rule in the Scope Guard family** ([[2026-08-30-codex-sol-scope-guard-rules]]): short, mechanical, checkable instructions about where agent output lands, instead of trusting the agent's default scatter-and-flat-folder instinct.
- **Prompts steer one output; scripts enforce every output** — Julian ([[2026-09-06-julian-risk-based-code-review]]) makes the complementary point with CI-enforced invariants. Agrawal's prompts are the lightweight steering layer; where a rule must hold long-term, it should graduate from prompt to check.
- **Directly adoptable here:** our heartbeats produce plan-heavy artifacts (hiring plans, roadmaps, briefs). A standing "now the 80% version" pass before presenting any plan to the user is a one-line habit that buys most of the benefit at near-zero cost.
- **Skepticism gates:** "without fail every time" is n=1 enthusiasm with no failure cases shown, and the follow-up was ~6h old at capture with no engagement evidence exposed — no saved-as-recipe bookmark signal yet. But the prompts are free to trial and trivially droppable; the test costs one plan cycle.
